title: Bond Yields Signal Fed Rate Hikes Ahead as Treasury Markets Flash Warning

body:
U.S. Treasury bond markets are sending unmistakable signals that the Federal Reserve may be forced to raise interest rates in the coming months, a prospect that was nearly unthinkable at the start of 2026 and one that carries significant consequences for NRI investors, the rupee, and Indian financial markets.

The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note has risen nearly 20 basis points since the start of July, hitting 4.621% earlier this week — the highest since May 19. Interest-rate-sensitive 2-year notes jumped nearly 18 basis points since the end of June, reaching 4.279%, a 16-month high, before easing on Friday to 4.137% after softer-than-expected inflation data.

Hawkish Fed Rhetoric Fuels the Move

The CME Group's FedWatch tool showed the odds of a rate hike at the Fed's July 28–29 meeting surging to 42% earlier this week, up from just 8% a month ago. While softer June CPI data subsequently collapsed those odds to 17%, the probability of a September hike remains near 50%, and nearly all traders expect at least one hike by year-end.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller warned that rate hikes could come "in the near term" if inflation pressures persist. "I am concerned about the equally plausible case that data in the coming weeks will show that inflation will remain at its elevated level or even trend higher, requiring tighter monetary policy," Waller said.

New Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, testifying before Congress, reaffirmed his commitment to price stability while maintaining his preference for no forward guidance, leaving markets to parse incoming data for clues. Minutes from his first Fed meeting revealed that members broadly agreed higher rates would be needed if inflation remains sticky.

Oil Prices Cloud the Inflation Outlook

The escalating U.S.-Iran conflict threatens to push inflation readings higher through the summer. Brent crude has climbed above $86 per barrel after President Trump intensified attacks on Iranian targets and vowed to control the Strait of Hormuz. Rising energy costs feed directly into headline inflation metrics, potentially forcing the Fed's hand even as core prices moderate.

Impact on NRI Deposits, the Rupee, and Indian Markets

A Fed rate hike would have direct implications for the Indian diaspora. NRI fixed deposits in Indian banks — a popular savings vehicle — could see reduced inflows as higher U.S. rates make dollar-denominated deposits more attractive. The rupee, already under pressure from rising oil import costs, would face additional headwinds from a stronger dollar.

Indian government bonds have shown resilience, however. The benchmark 6.94% 2036 bond yield eased to 6.7703% after softer U.S. inflation data cooled rate-hike expectations. Foreign investors have channeled approximately $4.2 billion into Indian bonds since June 1, buoyed by expectations that Indian debt will be included in Bloomberg's Global Aggregate Index.

Indian retail inflation rose to 4.38% in June, breaching the Reserve Bank of India's target for the first time in 17 months. But several brokerages have trimmed their rate-hike calls for India, expecting full-year inflation to average below the central bank's estimates. For NRI investors navigating both markets, the coming weeks of data — and the Fed's July 29 decision — will be pivotal.
author: Diaspora Desk
